lead: A wing behaves like a cantilever built into the fuselage. Lift pushes it up; wing structure, fuel and engines push it down. Integrating the net load from the tip inward gives the shear force; integrating again gives the bending moment. Both are zero at the free tip and usually largest at the root. These two diagrams are the first numbers a stress engineer needs: they show where the wing is worked hardest and what the carry-through structure must react.
prereq: You need: loads on aircraft for the load factor and the V-n diagram for the design cases.

blocks.text: Take the root at x = 0 and the tip at x = L. The semi-span L is in metres. The net load w(x) is in N/m and is positive upward. It is lift minus wing structure weight minus fuel weight per metre. A positive w means the net load bends the wing upward.

blocks.where: V is the shear force in N at station x; w is the net load per unit span in N/m, positive upward; x is distance from the root in m; L is the semi-span in m; ξ is a dummy span coordinate in m.
M is the bending moment in N·m at station x; V, w, x, L and ξ are as above. Use one sign convention throughout: upward net load positive, root at x = 0.

blocks.text: The part of the wing outboard of x carries all the net load beyond x. V(x) is the total of that outboard load. M(x) is that same load multiplied by its lever arm (ξ − x) about the station x. At the free tip there is no outboard load, so V(L) = 0 and M(L) = 0.

For a uniform net load w, V = w(L − x) and M = w(L − x)²/2. At the root V = wL and M = wL²/2. The moment rises with the square of the remaining span, so near the root it grows much faster than shear. That is why the root fitting and the carry-through structure are sized mainly by moment.
An engine, a store or a landing gear adds a downward point load: the shear jumps there and the moment changes slope, as worked example 2 shows.
Real lift is not uniform along the span: it depends on planform, twist and the trailing vortices. A first estimate gives the load shape the shear and moment integrals need.

An elliptic lift distribution has minimum induced drag for a given span and a given total lift. A rectangular wing carries less lift near its tips than its constant chord suggests, because the tip vortices unload them; a tapered wing carries more lift near the root because the chord is larger there. Schrenk's approximation takes the mean of the elliptic distribution and the planform distribution at each station.

blocks.where: w<sub>lift</sub> is the estimated lift per unit span in N/m; w<sub>ell</sub> is the elliptic distribution in N/m; w<sub>plan</sub> is the planform distribution in N/m, proportional to chord c(x); the constant of proportionality is chosen so the total lift equals the required lift.

blocks.text: Taper moves load inboard. A tapered wing of the same span and total lift has a lower root bending moment than a rectangular wing, because the centre of its lift sits closer to the root; the root shear, equal to the total net load, is the same. Use Schrenk's shape for preliminary loads, then replace it with wind-tunnel or CFD data when available. The integration method does not change.

sections.h3: Mass relief, carry-through and tail loads

blocks.text: Wing structure and fuel are not lift. Subtract them before integrating. This is mass relief: it lowers the root bending moment. Fuel in the wing gives strong relief when tanks are full, but the critical case may be low fuel, so check every fuel state from empty to full tanks. A full tank is not automatically the worst case.

The wing root moment is reacted by the carry-through structure and the fuselage frames at the attachment points. The carry-through is the structure that carries the wing root moment across the fuselage. The fuselage behaves as a beam: it receives a concentrated moment and shear at the wing junction, so its bending moment diagram has a jump there.

The tail produces a lift or downforce at a long arm from the centre of gravity. That tail load bends the rear fuselage. The bending moment is zero at the point where the load is applied and grows linearly forward along the fuselage, so it is largest at the wing attachment, where it equals T × l. The carry-through then reacts it. Here T is the tail load in N and l is the distance in m from the wing attachment to the line of action of the tail load. See stress analysis of fuselage and tail unit for how the cross-section carries it.

figure.caption: Shear (top) and bending moment (bottom) along the 8 m semi-span. Solid: the uniform 9 kN/m net load of worked example 1, 72 kN and 288 kN·m at the root. Dashed: with the 40 kN engine at 3 m the shear drops from 45 to 5 kN there and the root values fall to 32 kN and 168 kN·m.

spec.aria: Two stacked plots against distance from the root, 0 to 8 metres. Top: shear falls linearly from 72 kilonewtons at the root to zero at the tip; a dashed line for the engine case drops from 45 to 5 at 3 metres and reaches 32 at the root. Bottom: bending moment curves from 288 kilonewton metres at the root (162 at 2 metres) to zero at the tip; the dashed engine case is 112.5 at 3 metres and 168 at the root.

examples.question: A wing of semi-span 8 m carries a uniform lift of 12 kN/m and has wing structure and fuel of 3 kN/m along the same span. Find the shear force and bending moment at the root and at 2 m from the root.
steps: Net load per unit span: w = 12 − 3 = 9 kN/m.
Semi-span: L = 8 m. At the root x = 0, the outboard length is L − x = 8 m.
Root shear: V = w(L − x) = 9 × 8 = 72 kN.
Root moment: M = w(L − x)²/2 = 9 × 8²/2 = 9 × 64/2 = 288 kN·m.
At x = 2 m from the root, the outboard length is L − x = 6 m.
examples.answer: At the root: shear 72 kN and bending moment 288 kN·m. At 2 m from the root: shear 54 kN and bending moment 162 kN·m.

examples.question: The wing of the first example (semi-span 8 m, net distributed load 9 kN/m upward) also carries an engine 3 m from the root. At the design load factor the engine’s inertia load is 40 kN downward (an engine of about 1630 kg at n = 2.5). Find the shear force and bending moment at the root and on each side of the engine, and the largest shear on the span.
steps: Outboard of the engine (3 m < x ≤ 8 m) nothing changes: V = 9(8 − x) and M = 9(8 − x)²/2.
Just outboard of the engine, x = 3 m: V = 9 × 5 = 45 kN; M = 9 × 5² ÷ 2 = 112.5 kN·m.
Crossing the engine, the outboard load drops by 40 kN: just inboard of it, V = 45 − 40 = 5 kN. M does not jump: it is still 112.5 kN·m at x = 3 m.
Largest shear: 45 kN, just outboard of the engine, which is more than the 32 kN at the root.
examples.answer: Root shear 32 kN and root moment 168 kN·m; at the engine the shear jumps from 45 kN (outboard) to 5 kN (inboard) while M stays 112.5 kN·m. The largest shear, 45 kN, is at the engine station, not the root.

traps: Using lift alone and forgetting to subtract wing structure and fuel. The root moment comes out too high because mass relief is missing.
Applying M = wL²/2 to a tapered lift distribution or a wing with an engine. That formula is only for uniform w; integrate the actual w(x) and add each point load times its arm.
Forgetting the fuselage carry-through. The wing root moment does not disappear at the fuselage; it is reacted by the carry-through and frames.
Assuming full fuel is always critical. Fuel relief changes with the fuel load, so check every fuel state from empty to full.

quiz.q: Define net load per unit span w(x) for a wing and give its unit.
quiz.a: w(x) is lift per unit span minus wing structure weight per unit span minus fuel weight per unit span. It is in N/m and is positive upward.

quiz.q: A wing has semi-span 10 m and uniform net load 6 kN/m upward. Find the root shear force and root bending moment.
quiz.a: Root shear V = wL = 6 × 10 = 60 kN. Root moment M = wL²/2 = 6 × 10²/2 = 300 kN·m.

quiz.q: Explain how fuel in the wing changes the root bending moment, and why the full-fuel case may not be critical.
quiz.a: Fuel weight acts downward against the lift, so it relieves the root bending moment; full tanks give the most relief. A low-fuel case can therefore give a higher root moment and may be the critical one.

quiz.q: What is Schrenk's approximation for spanwise lift?
quiz.a: It estimates lift per unit span as the mean of the elliptic distribution and the planform distribution at each station. The planform part is proportional to chord, scaled so total lift matches the required lift.

quiz.q: Lift is 15 kN/m and wing structure plus fuel is 5 kN/m along a semi-span of 12 m. Find shear and bending moment at 3 m from the root.
quiz.a: Net load w = 15 − 5 = 10 kN/m. Remaining length = 12 − 3 = 9 m. V = 10 × 9 = 90 kN. M = 10 × 9²/2 = 405 kN·m.

quiz.q: A wing of semi-span 6 m has a uniform net load of 10 kN/m upward and an engine inertia load of 25 kN downward at 2 m from the root. Find the root shear and root moment.
quiz.a: Root shear = 10 × 6 − 25 = 35 kN. Root moment = 10 × 6² ÷ 2 − 25 × 2 = 180 − 50 = 130 kN·m.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry loads work uses panel methods or CFD for spanwise lift, then finite element models for internal loads. Active load alleviation, aeroelastic tailoring and gust load cases are active research areas. Certification loads are checked against flight-test measurements. Search for Schrenk approximation, wing bending moment diagram, mass relief wing loads and tail load fuselage bending.
